title: The teenage body clock
subtitle: Is adolescent sleepiness a matter of laziness or of biology? The evidence increasingly points one way.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every morning, in homes across the world, a familiar battle is fought. Parents call, knock and eventually pull back the curtains, while a teenager who seemed wide awake at midnight lies motionless under the duvet. For generations, this behaviour has been put down to idleness, late-night screens or simple rebellion. Over the past three decades, however, sleep scientists have assembled a substantial body of evidence suggesting that the problem is not primarily one of character. Adolescents, it appears, are biologically inclined to fall asleep and wake up later than either children or adults – and the timetables of most secondary schools take little account of that fact.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation lies largely in the body's internal clock, the circadian system, which regulates the daily rise and fall of hormones, body temperature and alertness. One of its key signals is melatonin, a hormone released by the brain in the evening that prepares the body for sleep. During puberty, the timing of melatonin release shifts later, typically by up to two hours. Dr Hannah Okafor, a sleep researcher who has studied several hundred teenagers in laboratory conditions, found that this shift occurred regardless of whether participants had access to phones or computers in the evening. 'You can take every device out of the bedroom,' she says, 'and a fifteen-year-old's brain will still not be ready for sleep at ten o'clock.'

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second mechanism reinforces the first. Throughout the waking day, a chemical called adenosine gradually accumulates in the brain, creating what researchers call 'sleep pressure'. In younger children this pressure builds rapidly, so that they become drowsy early in the evening. In adolescents, by contrast, it builds more slowly, allowing them to remain alert well into the night. Crucially, however, teenagers' need for sleep does not decline at the same time: most experts agree that they still require between eight and ten hours a night. A sixteen-year-old who cannot fall asleep before midnight but must get up at half past six is therefore losing at least two hours of sleep every school night, a deficit that weekend lie-ins can only partly repay.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consequences of this chronic shortfall extend well beyond yawning in morning lessons. Professor Martin Lindqvist, who has reviewed large-scale health surveys of secondary-school students, points out that those who regularly sleep fewer than seven hours are consistently more likely to report symptoms of anxiety and low mood. Insufficient sleep has also been linked to weight gain, weakened immunity and poorer control of emotions. Newly qualified drivers are especially at risk: drowsiness slows reaction times in much the same way as alcohol, and young motorists are over-represented in accidents caused by falling asleep at the wheel.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the biology cannot be changed, the timetable can. One of the earliest and most influential experiments took place in Minnesota in the late 1990s, when several school districts moved the start of the high-school day from around 7.15 to 8.30 a.m. or later. Researchers who followed the students found that they did not simply stay up later to compensate, as critics had predicted; instead they gained close to an hour of extra sleep on school nights. Teachers reported that pupils were more alert in early lessons, and attendance improved. Since then, similar changes have been studied in dozens of locations. In one city on the west coast of the United States, a delay of just under an hour produced an average gain of 34 minutes of sleep a night, along with better attendance and a modest rise in grades.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most persuasive evidence comes from outside the classroom. A widely cited study from Kentucky examined road-traffic data in a county where secondary schools had put back their opening time by an hour. In the two years after the change, the crash rate among teenage drivers fell by around 16 per cent, while in the rest of the state, where schools kept the earlier start, it actually rose. Dr Sofia Marquez, a public-health specialist, notes that findings of this kind are difficult to explain in any other way, since few other factors changed in the county at the time.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Opponents point to the practical costs: bus routes must be reorganised, after-school sports and part-time jobs finish later, and parents who start work early may struggle with childcare for younger siblings, whose schools are often made to open earlier so that buses can be shared. Dr James Whitfield, an education economist, has argued that the academic gains, while genuine, are smaller than campaigners sometimes claim, and that the money involved might achieve more if spent elsewhere. Yet the weight of evidence has shifted policy nonetheless. In 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that secondary schools begin no earlier than 8.30 a.m., and in 2019 California became the first US state to write a similar rule into law.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Researchers stress that a later bell is not a cure-all. Professor Anika Rao, who studies adolescent behaviour, points out that bright light late in the evening, including the light from screens, can push the body clock later still, so that good habits at home remain important. Exposure to daylight in the morning, by contrast, helps to pull the clock earlier. 'The school timetable is not the only factor,' she says, 'but it is the one factor that society, rather than individual families, can actually control.'
